title: Afraid, and Trusting Anyway
overview: A person hunted by enemies admits their fear, keeps choosing to trust God, and looks ahead to giving thanks for rescue.

parts.label: Hunted from every side (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The writer feels surrounded by many proud attackers who will not let up, day after day. The psalm's heading links it to David being seized by the Philistines in the city of Gath while he was running from King Saul (1 Samuel 21).

parts.label: Fear and trust together (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: The writer does not claim to be fearless; trust is what they reach for at the very moment fear arrives. In verse 4 the word for the attackers is literally 'flesh,' a reminder that even dangerous people are frail and limited.

parts.label: Twisted words and hidden plots (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: The enemies spin everything the writer says into something bad, hide, and track every move, hoping to kill. The writer bluntly asks God to bring them down in anger, a raw plea for justice that the psalm does not soften.

parts.label: Tears kept and counted (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: The writer pictures God keeping track of every restless move in exile and storing each tear in a bottle or writing it in a book, so that no sorrow goes unnoticed. Scholars are unsure whether this draws on a real custom of saving tears, but the point is clear: God is for me.

parts.label: The refrain repeated (vv. 10-11)
parts.note: The chorus from verse 4 comes back, now also using God's personal name, the LORD. Saying it a second time works like holding on to a steady truth while the danger is still there.

parts.label: Promised thanks (vv. 12-13)
parts.note: People in danger often vowed to bring a thank offering, a sacrifice of gratitude often shared as a meal before God, once they were rescued. The writer means to keep that promise, grateful to be spared from death and free to go on living in God's presence among the living.

think: When you are afraid, what do you find yourself leaning on, and how well does it hold?
